en: The Scripture on the Universal Gate Chapter, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly.

The assembly accompanying the Buddha consisted of eight hundred bhikṣus and forty-two thousand bodhisattvas—those who had attained all dhāraṇīs, perfected the supernormal powers, whose noble wisdom was vast and flowing, whose eloquence was unimpeded, whose samādhis were firmly established, and who were not limited in their extensive learning.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Vimalagarbha, who, together with ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas, came from the land of the Tathāgata Samantakusuma. That world is named Viśuddhacaryā; they were currently traveling here, desiring to go to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the Sahā world to seek instruction and receive teachings.

At that time, the Buddha saw from afar and smiled; from his mouth issued flames of light with extraordinary and marvelous colors, universally illuminating the ten directions so that both the internal and external were clearly transparent and nothing was not reached.

At that time, the Great Being, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra-kumārabhūta, rose within the great assembly, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why do you smile?
This smile contains a profound and subtle meaning that is not understood by the world, nor can it be sustained by ordinary bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; your compassion is indeed such as this.
"O Honored One, there must be a specific meaning for your smile; we pray that you will reveal what we have not yet attained, for all of us likewise desire to hear it.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Prabhūtaratna:
"To the east of here, beyond immeasurable, innumerable, incalculable, and asaṃkhyeya hundreds of thousands of koṭis of worlds, there is a world named Viśuddhacaryā."

That Buddha is named Samantakusuma Tathāgata; he is constantly surrounded by countless billions of hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and together they discourse upon the dharma of non-retrogression and the inconceivable.
There was a venerable bodhisattva named Vimalagarbha, surrounded by a retinue of countless thousands of great bodhisattvas, who traveled through the void with his robes fluttering as he walked.

The Buddha thought to himself of this Vimalagarbha, who had traveled through distant lands by various routes; he was sent to receive the "Universal Gate" chapter by the command of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Samantakusuma, and would now soon return to join the assembly of bodhisattvas.

At that time, the Great Sage, manifesting his teachings according to their respective forms and appearing in accordance with all needs, caused the assemblies of bodhisattvas from countless and limitless worlds to arrive immediately; they came to this Sahā world and proceeded to the realm of Mahābrahmā.
"Therefore, I smiled!

As soon as he had finished speaking, the Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha and the great assembly suddenly vanished from that place and arrived here at Vulture Peak Mountain. Surrounded by their retinue, they proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
All the bodhisattvas dwelling in leisure and tranquility upon this Vulture Peak Mountain gathered together; having paid their respects, they withdrew and took their seats.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha, in accordance with the occasion, manifested seven-jeweled lotuses with a thousand petals each. Carrying them to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, he prostrated himself and presented them, saying:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Samantakusuma, from the world-system Viśuddhacaryā, respectfully inquires after your health."
“I have traveled immeasurable distances with vigor and strength, my faculties are light and agile, and my daily life is peaceful and secure; I have brought much relief to others.
Now I have been sent here to convey my respectful greetings and to receive the inconceivable and pure chapters, such as the *Samantamukha-parivarta*, to be expounded for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
Then, having completed his inquiries, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalagarbha withdrew into the void and sat cross-legged, together with the other bodhisattvas, upon jeweled lotus flowers.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī rose from within the great assembly, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
I pray that you will explain the source of the Dharma of the inconceivable path of the "Universal Gate" chapter, and expound it in detail for the sake of the bodhisattvas!

I recall that in the remote past, during a time long ago, from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Samantavairocana, I heard this sūtra and gave rise to eighty-four million hundred thousand *koṭis* of *nayutas* of samādhis, and further attained seventy-seven million hundred thousand *nayutas* of gateways to dhāraṇīs.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the bodhisattvas, will proclaim this once more.
The Buddha told Pǔshǒu Tóngzhēn:
"Listen attentively and reflect upon it well!"
"I shall now, for your sake, fully explain the inconceivable secret treasure within the inner treasury of the Universal Gate.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and his great assembly all replied together:
"Yes, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
At that time, Puṣya the Youth and the various bodhisattvas received the instruction with single-minded attention and listened.
The Buddha addressed Puṣya:
“If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to study the dharmas entered through the Universal Gateway, they should practice equanimity toward forms,
practice equanimity toward sounds, practice equanimity toward odors, practice equanimity toward tastes, practice equanimity toward tactile objects,
practice equanimity toward the realm of the mind, practice equanimity toward women, and practice equanimity toward men.”
They roam among young girls, they roam among boys, they roam among the devas, they roam among the nāgas, they roam among the yakṣas,
they roam among the gandharvas, they roam among the asuras, they roam among the garuḍas,
they roam among the kiṃnaras, they roam among the mahoragas, and they roam among those in the hells.
They wander equally among hungry ghosts, they wander equally among animals, they wander equally amidst lust, they wander equally amidst anger,
they wander equally amidst ignorance; they wander equally amidst all that is wholesome, they wander equally amidst the roots of all virtues, they wander equally amidst all conditioned phenomena,
and they wander equally amidst all unconditioned phenomena.
Thus it is, Puṣya! The manner in which all bodhisattvas circulate is like this:

they are entirely equal, dwelling in equanimity; they are fully endowed with the ultimate Way and do not turn back; they universally enter the essentials of the Dharma—profound, subtle, and singularly esoteric—which is empty, non-existent, and tranquil. This is the method for training in and entering the Samādhi of the Universal Gate.
The Buddha addressed the youth Viśeṣacintin:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva who dwells in equanimity regarding form?

To understand form clearly as being like a bubble on water—unobtainable, incapable of being maintained, and lacking solidity—and thus to contemplate with an equanimous mind that no form exists: this is called a bodhisattva dwelling in equanimity regarding form."
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by 'the bodhisattva’s equal engagement with sounds'?
It is like the sound of a person's call that elicits an echo; it immediately vanishes, leaving no form or image, and its destination is unknown."

All things are without multiplicity and without distinction; they are also without marks. Having realized that there are no marks, one understands that what people speak of is empty and without reality. Once one comprehends that all sounds are like echoes in the deep mountains, one is then able to contemplate them with equanimity; this is the bodhisattva’s equal engagement with sounds.
He further addressed Pu-shou: "What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s equanimous wandering amidst foul and fragrant odors?

For hundreds of billions of kalpas, he circulates back and forth; though his nose smells them, he never grows weary. When various perfumes come toward him as intensely as wind and rain, they all gather and return to his body, yet like the depths of the great ocean, there is no sense of being filled. The manifestations of these fragrances are impermanent and undergo a hundred transformations; their transformations are like illusions, having no root or origin. Sometimes they may disturb the Way and its Virtue (moral conduct) and cannot be restrained. Such, then, are the phenomena of falsehood!"
There is no ultimate truth; even if one seeks to examine it, there is no point of convergence.

Judging by this principle, these things are non-existent and cannot be grasped; they are void and without reality, as fleeting as empty space, like illusions or transformations, possessing no original form. It is through the conditions of mental images, perceptions, and attachments that forms arise. If one can discern their emptiness and lack of reality, this constitutes the Bodhisattva’s impartial contemplation, whereby one traverses both the foul and the fragrant.
He further addressed Pu-shou:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equanimous engagement with all flavors?
Upon reaching the throat, one does not perceive the taste of saltiness, nor is there any absence of flavor."
Through the discrimination of causes and conditions, it is merely what the tongue finds sweet!
Due to the convergence of conditions, hundreds of thousands of flavors arise; these are but illusory transformations.
That which is produced from the earth has a nourishment of a single flavor, without any diversity.

"To clearly understand and awaken to this, being without conceptualization or thought, and finding equal sweetness in all things—this is what it means for a bodhisattva to practice equanimous contemplation while traversing various flavors.
He then addressed Pu-shou:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing equanimous traversal regarding the tactile?"

When the mind has a certain object of intent, it seeks it through conditions; yet though the body may be adorned with fine fabrics and enhanced by beautiful colors, rare treasures, and extraordinary wonders—things that are soft and delicate—they cannot be obtained. Having fully understood these conditions, one finds that neither the subtle, smooth, nor the coarse textures have any place to abide, nor do they give rise to attachment.

Upon careful consideration, tactile sensations are of no benefit; they are the desires of this world, craved by the ignorant and the wicked, and serve as the very foundation of birth and death—all of which arise from these.
A wise and great being recognizes their faults and does not engage with them, remaining forever free from affliction throughout all lifetimes.
All that is borne by the earth belongs to the same category and is without distinction;

yet, driven by the perceptions of sound and form, people act perversely, causing themselves to assume various different appearances and dress accordingly, thereby deluding themselves regarding the Way and its Virtue and failing to associate with the worthy and the virtuous.
The realized one awakens to this and does not engage in such affairs.

Dwelling in seclusion, clad in coarse cloth yet harboring wisdom within, he appears as a fool to the outside world while inwardly cherishing a bright pearl. For billions of kalpas, he is of one body with the Way; far removed from the notion of "self," he is likewise free from the thought of "mine. Thus, the subtle and smooth [sensations] and the self are both identical.
It is neither empty nor substantial; it is like an illusion and like a magical transformation. It has no basis and no place of abiding.

Because of attachment to clothing, one comes to rely upon them; yet the realized person, beholding this, perceives that nothing exists. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva’s equanimous contemplation while moving among tactile sensations.
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equanimous wandering in the mental dharmas?
As for 'mental dharmas,' they are the guardians of the people within the triple world."

They comforted and exhorted them with joy, causing them all to assemble; they settled them through virtue, encouraged them through skillful means, and bestowed upon them wisdom. They universally cultivated the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), remaining serenely established in one place within the three realms, neither joining nor parting, causing their minds to be held forever so that no location could be known.
They perceived neither forms nor sounds coming and going, nor did they harbor any hesitation.
As it should be according to the mind, the assembly neither gathers nor disperses; it knows no place of abiding, nor does it go anywhere.

If it manifests various kinds of forms, each form being distinct, yet within there is no location, and even that location has no fixed abiding. It is like a phantom and like a magical creation—empty, non-existent, without location, and with no location where it might abide.

When the realized one beholds this, he perceives that there is nothing at all; he then maintains his own mind, free from thought and free from seeking. He sees as if not seeing, hears as if not hearing, and remains serenely self-abiding. This is called the Bodhisattva’s impartial contemplation as he wanders within the dharmas of the mind.
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equanimous wandering within the mind?
When the mind wanders toward women, one examines the four great elements and finds that there is no woman."
Those whose wills are deluded by folly are entirely devoted to sensual desire and distracted by emptiness; yet their essence is one and the same, and there is nothing therein that can be defiled.

To reckon that there is a woman is like a magician conjuring a human form, which bows, sways, and bends according to the movements of others' minds. Following what they do and according to what they enjoy, women are like illusions; though one gives rise to thoughts of lustful desire, there is no such woman there.

Human beings are fundamentally equal, yet they are deluded by ignorance; their minds follow desire, and desire leads to craving. Craving results in attachment to this world, which must not be left unrestrained; one must urgently apply the bit and bridle to discipline it.
The wise person penetrates this: they discern that all things are like space; space is neither quiescent nor possesses form.
Conditioned arising occurs through opposition; where there is no opposition, there is no arising.
"If one can discern in this manner, this is what is called a bodhisattva’s impartial contemplation while roaming within the mental states of women.
He further addressed Pu-shou:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s impartial roaming within the pure dharmas?"

Purity is like a man. Just as one might cause a man to generate his own intention, with a mind like a diamond, focused and uniquely heroic and fierce, he contemplates this woman; yet his desire-mind is formless, for its reality cannot be grasped, nor does it manifest as the image of a woman or the like—it is merely the various forms and desires that give rise to the perception of a woman.
If one contemplates those thoughts of desire—whether regarding men or women—as being like a mirage or the moon reflected in water, then for one who observes in this way, there are no men or women.

They are entirely devoid of male form, and women are likewise; they exist as mere falsehoods, lacking any lasting endurance. They are but illusory manifestations, appearing suddenly and then vanishing.

Because they are able to discern and cognize the male mind and the female mind—realizing that these two are empty and non-existent—and having attained equanimity, they can manifest as a woman and then transform back into a man.
"This is what is meant by a bodhisattva’s impartial contemplation while roaming within the pure dharma of men.
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s impartial roaming among boys and girls?"

Just as when the roots of a tree are uprooted, the sprouts will never grow again; so too, when the mind no longer arises, one attains cessation from this point on. For the wise, there is no seeking for a fruit, nor can a fruit be obtained.

If there are those of noble lineage who are sons of the wise, who are discerning in their deliberations and understand how to give rise to all thoughts of valor while remaining free from conceptualization—like a withered tree that produces neither flowers nor fruit, like a dried-up river whose waters no longer flow—such as these, toward boys and girls, manifest such equality as the sky, which is devoid of reality. They perceive that woman is fundamentally pure, they perceive that man is fundamentally pure, and they perceive that *nirvāṇa* is fundamentally pure. Those who are thus able to contemplate with equanimity move among boys and girls.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s 'even wandering' as a young boy?

It is like a tree: if there are no sprouts, there will be no roots or trunk; if there are no roots or trunk, there will be no flowers or fruit; and if there are no flowers or fruit, there will be no name for the fruit."

Women are thus; if there were no women, there would be no men. When one is equal toward both men and women, there is no self (*ātman*). Names and designations arise from conditions and are conceived through ignorance. To realize that womanhood is unarisen and lacks the nature of a son, and to understand that all persons are non-existent—this non-existence is equality, which is equanimity.
"This is what is meant by the Bodhisattva Samadarśin thus roaming among young boys.
He then addressed Puṣya:
"What is meant by a Bodhisattva roaming among the devas?"

The merits of the various devas are spontaneously pure; their intentions are fresh and clean, their minds are pure and their speech is pure, being without blemish or defilement. Their palaces are exquisitely adorned without being constructed, and the wondrous flowers of the trees of their hearts bloom without being planted. Their merit and virtue are spontaneous, like an illusion or a transformation; their birth is inconceivable. With pure light and lapis lazuli, they are liberated through purity and clarity, and yet there is no corpse or spirit. Being empty and non-existent, they establish themselves as the heavens with artificial forms; their natural physical forms appear in a state of vagueness. Their supreme teaching of equality manifests the images of the various devas; this is what is meant by "emptiness," which does not rely on external metaphors.

Upon examining the internal contemplation through the thirty-two heavens, one finds that the number of palaces and towers is natural and spontaneous; no one can see them, for only those who have attained the Way know them.
"Therefore, the Bodhisattva deeply contemplates that the internal and external are equal and without distinction; this is what is meant by the Bodhisattva’s 'equal wandering among the devas.
He further addressed Pṛthuśāsana:
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s 'equal wandering among the nāgas'?"

Seeing clouds arise where there was no water for seven days, the rain that fell moistened and bathed everything without exception; neither remaining outside nor inside, it pervaded Jambudvīpa and gradually returned to the great ocean, the source from which all water comes.

Sentient beings are likewise; they study various conditions, and by depending on these, they give rise to many cravings that lead to the emergence of sorrow. They manifest countless and diverse offenses. Examining this through internal contemplation, one observes: from where does anger arise?

Dragons turn back and sea-monsters are startled; every person is thus. Heaven collapses and earth is rent asunder, yet all arise from the dragon. If the inner dragon does not turn back and the outer dragon does not follow, there can be no spontaneous fortune, and sentient beings would cease to exist.
The ignorant and deluded regard the unreal as real;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives dragons as equal, with inner and outer in harmony, and compassion identical for all.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s equal wandering among dragons.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equal engagement with ghosts and spirits?
Their mind is like an open door; it possesses form and appearance, its body is tall and vast, beyond reach, and all thoughts converge as one."
Among the hundreds of thousands of the multitude, there is likewise no physical form; it is only through sound and resonance that they respond.
It is like drinking poison, which brings about one's own ruin.
Their minds are of a single kind, yet they have nothing to fear; this is entirely due to their self-indulgence, as they wander, plunder, and act with total license.
Obstructed by difficulties and faced with fear, one realizes that this dharma has no reality.
All manifold perceptions converge and return; these perceptions are inconceivable, being unreal and merely empty discourse.
Consider this: when observing internally, from where do ghosts and spirits arise?
Within, there are hundreds and thousands of such spirits; without, it is likewise.
If fear is not aroused within, then there will be no dread without.
Within, he felt no sorrow; without, no tears fell.
Internally, he gave rise to thoughts of ghosts and spirits; externally, there appeared hundreds and thousands of ghostly beings, all of whom came to take refuge in him.
Because of this, they fall ill or even die, undergoing immeasurable suffering; all of this arises from a deviant mind that is not upright.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva realizes that things are empty and non-existent, and that there are no ghosts or spirits, understanding that everything arises from the mind, they are then able to maintain an equanimous and pure mind. With their intent tranquil, equanimous, and not deviant, there is consequently no one who can harm the Bodhisattva.

If one manifests various transformations such as the forms of ghosts and spirits, yet internally observes that there are ultimately no such ghosts or spirits, and the external manifestations consequently vanish—this is what is meant.
This is called the bodhisattva’s equal wandering among ghosts and spirits.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equanimous wandering among the gandharvas?

Their dharmas are without intrinsic nature, yet they proceed through vocal expression; one understands that there is neither coming nor going, nor is there any returning. They are like space, formless, appearing only as they follow sound."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva observes within himself, if there is no consciousness of perception, then there are no gandharvas; for the gandharva is the leader of the ghosts and spirits.
With no thoughts arising within and no perverse notions without, by what cause do these various ailments thus converge?
As for the gandharvas, they have names but no forms; their voices come and go, yet no one can see them.
The essence of these teachings is that they are ultimately non-existent.
As for the Gandharvas, they are empty and without reality; the Bodhisattva observes them as such, seeing them as resulting from illusion and transformation.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to roam equally among the gandharvas.
He then addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva roaming equally among the asuras?"
Because there is evidence for this matter, the minds of the asuras are equal: they neither arise nor cease, they are neither born nor exhausted, and thus manifest equality.
All instances of anger and poisonous intent originate from the asuras.
Āraṇa is a nāga deity who, though possessing much envy, manifests equanimity; this is the bodhisattva’s impartial contemplation as he dwells among the asuras as their mental object.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equal wandering among the garuḍas?

To address and establish names and titles—were it not for name-and-form (nāmarūpa), there would be no such thing; yet name-and-form arises through the tongue, and from the tongue comes calamity, establishing the very root of transgression."

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva studies profound wisdom that reaches far; he realizes that all things are empty and non-existent, like these illusory transformations that take form according to the mind. There is no one who sees them, for the coming and going of sounds is due to frailty!

When the mind is not upright, it thus manifests transformations of hundreds of thousands of millions of beings; yet upon examining them internally through successive observation, both are empty and non-existent!
When a bodhisattva contemplates with equanimity that there is no garuḍa, this is called the bodhisattva’s contemplation of equanimity while roaming among garuḍas.
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by 'the bodhisattva’s equal engagement with the Cāturmahārājika heaven'?
The Dharma is without action yet it acts; it neither acts nor does not act, yet it is able to establish things and also able to destroy them."
Soaring through the void, there is none who can equal him; thus he is named Candrahāsa (the Moon-Holder).

Everything proceeds from the hand, for the hand performs all tasks. When the mind gives rise to movement in the hand, and that movement transgresses the Mahāyāna, it causes one to undergo the sufferings of hell—all of which is due to Candrahāsa.

If a bodhisattva discriminates a non-arising multitude of beings and remains detached from active engagement, his hands do not move of their own accord; for what reason, then, would there be a *candāla*? According to the sequence of internal contemplation: if one does not move, one does not shake;

if one does not arise, one does not cease; if one is not born, one does not die. Internal movement gives rise to external manifestation; when the mind runs toward the hands, one engages in activity. Activity leads to falling into suffering; falling into suffering leads to having illness; those who have illness all have *yakṣas* (ghosts and spirits); these *yakṣas* are precisely the *candālas*!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thoroughly understands emptiness; it is empty and yet further empty, devoid of both emptiness and reality. He contemplates the *candāla* with equanimity:
all things arise through transformation and possess no form of true dharma. Since all activities are equal, there is no such thing as a *candāla*.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to practice equal contemplation while roaming among the *cāturmahārājika* devas.
He then addressed Puṣya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing equal roaming among the *mahoragas*?"

Regarding the names assigned to these dharmas: they establish various individuals, and there are no diverse forms that do not arise through them. According to the fundamental categories of persons and their respective numerical classes, various dharmas are manifested; all are established because they are given names based on their forms. Yet, these dharmas possess no inherent existence; such is merely their functional designation.
When embodied, he is the *uraga*; when detached from form, he is the *mahoraga*. That which is conceived is emptiness, yet the Way is perfected within the breast.

When the breast holds the great mandate and the mind is upright, one attains the realization of the Way. By discerning all conceptual perceptions and consciousnesses, all thoughts likewise cease. Through non-conceptualization, one reaches spontaneity; thus, he speaks only with a voice of equanimity. To sever and resolve all doubts for all beings, he manifests as the *mahoraga*.
This is the Bodhisattva’s profound entry into equal contemplation.
Examining the sequence of internal observation, there is nothing that arises within and nothing that is produced without; thus, even the name "Mahoraga" does not exist!
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to practice equal contemplation while roaming among the mahoragas.
He then addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing equal roaming within the hells?"

When dharmas do not exist, there are no hells; it is through the formation of perceptions and consciousness that hell arises. Hell has no master; those who seek it find it spontaneously, like an echo responding to a call or a fly flying into a lamp flame—such is the natural law, and nothing can save them.
Why is this so? It is because body and speech invite it, and thus it naturally arrives in response. There is no creator in the void; it arises from what one’s own thoughts bestow.

Since these thoughts have no inherent existence, they return to emptiness and return to emptiness. The conditions for calamity and suffering arise from oneself; if one is personally virtuous and disciplined, illness has no way to enter.
With no transgressions of body or speech and no deaths, the hells are pure, pristine, and stainless.
It is because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas lack the conditions for hell that they do not fear birth and death.
Why is this? Because they do not transgress the prohibitions.

They know that perceptions are like illusions and are likewise non-existent; although they establish various marks, those marks are non-existent and they do not cling to marks, nor is there the absence of marks. Since marks are non-existent, they are like illusory transformations appearing as elephants.

Those who behold these signs are without exception filled with joy; their joy leads to great compassion, through which they ascend to the Great Vow. This vow is distinct yet equal to space, profoundly tranquil, and yet it manifests the various sufferings and afflictions of the hells.

Examining the sequence of internal contemplation, one finds that the mouth brings resentment upon the body; the mouth is the door to hell, for it only enters and does not exit. What enters is immediately consumed and exhausted, while what exits becomes mere soil. Thus, through such diligent suffering, one must undergo further eons of rebirth.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva keeps his mouth closed and does not speak; he does not consult others with his mouth regarding what he eats, nor does he engage in idle speech, but remains tranquil and self-possessed. He does not enter assemblies, does not claim things as his own, speaks no double-tongued words, and endures all that is done to him.
When the Bodhisattva acts in this way, there is no hell for him.
The causes for rebirth in hell arise solely from the mouth; as words issue forth, one enters into transgression, and there is no escape from this affliction.

A Bodhisattva guards the mouth without discriminating between flavors; with compassion equal toward all, without partiality or softness, they consume food merely to sustain the body and maintain its form.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to practice equal contemplation while roaming through the hells.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva roaming equally among the hungry ghosts?"

Hungry ghosts have no form and no name; they originally have no location and no place of abode. They exist because of stinginess and are brought about by greed, yet stinginess itself has no dwelling place.

Not understanding all that exists and not knowing the Great Dharma, they reckon there is a self and do not perceive impermanence. Though their fame may reach hundreds of millions, when old age finally sets in, they proceed from stinginess to greed, from greed to desire, from desire to craving, from craving to attachment, from attachment to sorrow, from sorrow to suffering, from suffering to pain, from pain to fetters, from fetters to illness, and from illness to the place of death.

Among the three hardships, they obtain neither food nor clothing; their bodies are naked and they suffer from hunger and thirst, unable to find even water or drink. They are designated by the title and name "hungry ghosts" (preta).
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows that these are fundamentally non-existent and understands that there are no hungry ghosts at all; they are as tranquil as empty space.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva constantly practices equanimity; even when the nose encounters various fragrances, he does not inhale them, nor does he have any longing or delight for them.

Stinginess enters through the nose and brings about such great calamity. The nose is the essence of the mind's unified turbidity; yet, it neither enters nor exits, and by not receiving fragrant forms, one has nothing to covet. If there is no coveting, then there is no stinginess or grasping.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to contemplate hungry ghosts with equanimity.
He then addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva roaming among animals with equanimity?"
In the Dharma, there are no such things as animals; they arise from causes and conditions like clouds and mist, manifesting various forms with distinct colors.

Seeing them, one feels joy and gives rise to conceptualization; through the arising and ceasing of birth and death, anger emerges from within. From these thoughts and perceptions, the twelve links of dependent origination become attached; these knots remain unloosed, leading one to the realm of animals.
That [self] has no roots and is entirely non-existent; the mind and thoughts are empty and void, all arising from the various forms (*rūpa*).

Form, as the root of qualities, rushes through the five realms of existence, wandering through birth and death and assuming countless bodies—sometimes becoming a flying bird, sometimes a running beast.

The names "emptiness" and "impermanence" are established based on forms; they are like mists and clouds, appearing as various colors and images. The dispositions of animals, their transgressions and blessings, are like illusions—delusive and false—and yet one speaks of them as having animal forms.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva reckons that there is no self and realizes that there are no names; when his eyes first behold forms, his mind does not crave them, his heart does not dwell upon them, and his body does not seek advantage from them.

By means of these four kinds of equanimity, the bodhisattva also contemplates internal and external forms; flying through the ten directions to the most remote and dark places, there is nowhere they do not penetrate, all of which enters and exits through the eye.
The eye is the essence of the sun and moon and has two names:
when it enters into form, it is called the Golden-Winged Bird (Garuḍa); when it emerges from form, it is called Mañjuśrī.

According to the sequence of internal contemplation, all names enter through the eye; that which stirs the root of birth and death and acts perversely arises entirely from the Golden-Winged Bird, and is therefore designated as a beast.
The various classes of sentient beings among the animals—those that crawl, those that breathe, and those that slither—all such transformations are termed "animals.

When a Bodhisattva contemplates the human body as a whole, it likewise constitutes a trichiliocosm; within this world-system there are ten billion lands, so numerous that they cannot be calculated one by one. Above are the Thirty-three Heavens, and below extends to the Vajra-land; between them lie the eighteen hardships of the great hells.

In the abodes of the various devas and human beings, there are respective palaces and dwellings for non-humans, ghosts and spirits, dragons, birds, beasts, and even down to trees, grasses, and weeds; all those belonging to the realm of form reside within the human body. If their numbers are equal and balanced, the person will be short-lived;
if each thing corresponds perfectly without discrepancy, the person will be intelligent and possessed of wisdom.

If one encounters thieves, tigers, wolves, or venomous beasts; or falls into a ditch or pit; or is obstructed by trees; or is harmed by snakes or dogs—all such things arise from external conditions. Should there be a collapse of the body or the shattering of the limbs, one must examine the present circumstances and must not rely on or dwell upon past宿仇 (karmic enmity from previous lives); rather, one should reflect upon this both internally and externally.

The arising and ceasing brought about by past karma casts one into the realm of blindness and darkness; whether internal sentient beings or external sentient beings, internal forms or external forms, they are all equal and without distinction—every person is thus.
When evil intent arises within, external circumstances come to correspond with it; when there is a rebellious minister within, external ministers will likewise rebel, bringing harm upon the person.
The foolish person cannot know this for themselves, but instead sits and blames ghosts and spirits, when everything is actually caused by form (*rūpa*).

That which enters the eyes serves as a scout for the mind; its presiding name is "Hundred Evils. Any joy that delights the heart will inevitably entail subsequent calamity; everything proceeds from this.
To cause these animals and others to hear the sound of tranquility—this is what it means for a bodhisattva to roam equally among animals.
He further addressed Pu-shou:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva roaming equally amidst lust?”

The Dharma is free from lustful desire; it arises from causes and conditions. Through dependent origination, greed is brought about; one craves sensual desires, and these desires arise from mental conceptions. Yet that which is conceived is devoid of conception, like empty space—empty and without location. Because of desire, delusion ensues; this robs and disturbs the original nature, establishing the root of anxiety and suffering.
Covetous lust is like space; its location cannot be found. It follows form like a shadow and follows sound like an echo; it has no reality and no image, and thus it cannot be apprehended.
The foolish are deluded, their thoughts clouded by the defilements of worldly toil.

The Dharma is free from dust and stain; it is empty, signless, and tranquil. Desire is as void as space, and there is no one capable of exhausting it through rescue; even if one were to search throughout the ten directions, it could not be found.

Lust has no form, yet it is that which the ignorant and deluded crave; through greed they bring about their own ruin, losing their human form. Fearing a lack of peace, they hide themselves away, parting from the world in sorrow, never to meet again for all eternity.

If one were like a wild beast constantly harboring fear and anxiety—just as a man facing an enemy flees out of dread, abandoning his post and running away in the hope, "May they not see me!"—[then one would be like this].

The self is also empty; though one runs to exhaustion, there is no one to follow. To needlessly afflict one’s own body and endure such toil is likewise empty, for even the affection of one's household is but emptiness.

However, because people cherish and long for [desires] due to greed, desire becomes the anxiety of confinement in a prison; yet desire can also be a fierce resolve to care for all living beings. By remaining free from lustful excess, one will be without any affliction; the omens of inner evil will vanish, and everyone shall attain peace and security.
All things are empty and non-existent; emptiness itself is further emptied, for such a state has never existed.

They possess no liberation, yet out of folly and perversion, they instead proclaim themselves to be shrouded in the darkness of conceptualization, failing to understand that all phenomena are like space—neither existing nor perishing.

The Buddhas of the past, future, and present understand all forms of craving; yet craving is without liberation, for its fetters reside within manifold difficulties. Love and desire are entirely empty, void, and without reality. To censure lustful craving is to seek liberation from desire; one who seeks liberation from desire does not give rise to dualistic thoughts.

All these are without foundation; their very foundation is the absence of a foundation. This fundamental nature is spontaneously pure and free from defilement, like the Buddha’s place of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), which is equal and free from conceptualization.

Those who behold lustful excess do not escape calamity; those who follow such tranquility aspire to the departure from desire. When all that is conceived is empty, one then departs from all conceptualizations.

As for the thought that has been aroused, it is a thought of non-thought; one thus escapes from greed and lust. This means that when one transcends the perception of desire and has nothing to seek, one does not harbor the notion of an original limit. When there is no thought of greed and desire, the fundamental purity is such as this; thus, one does not even conceive of liberation. Even if one were to transcend desire, it would simply be called purity.
Craving is empty and non-existent; one should reckon this as non-dual. The ignorant and deluded, failing to understand, create the notion of duality.
In reality, dharmas have neither male nor female; they are of one equal essence. Heaven is the father and earth is the mother; among those born of heaven and earth, what difference can there be?

When Bodhisattvas practice with equanimity, they have no seeking for male or female; like illusions and transformations, their essence from beginning to end is thus. To perceive a distinction between male and female is to depart from the fundamental; this is to lose the words of the Dharma, to give rise to various conceptualizations, and for the net of afflictions to descend and burn. When greed and desire do not arise, and one does not produce conceptual thoughts, then there is no net of afflictions. Without burning the fetters, the net is not untied; yet, for one who understands greed and lust, these are merely provisional names—desire is undefiled by attachment. Knowing that all names are unimpeded, one finds that desire is neither existent nor non-existent. Perceiving the ultimate truth, one does not harbor thoughts of quietistic cultivation; with an impartial will toward the internal and external, there is no false view.

One who possesses desire knows that liberation cannot be attained; yet desire for the Buddha-dharma is equal to nirvana. By understanding and eliminating desire, one is equally free from the notion of self; knowing that desire is quiescent, one is equal to the art of serenity.

Examining the sequence of internal contemplation, all desires follow the ear; the ear and the mind communicate with one another, successively receiving and transmitting them. One who is courageous and fierce such that none can withstand him subdues everything without exception;
he has two names: when entering desire, he is the Lion King; when emerging from desire, he is Vimalakīrti.
He emerges from the three realms yet there is nowhere he does not enter and nowhere he does not emerge.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva is equal toward the pure and the defiled; his ears do not receive the five sounds, and he acts as a guide for all that is above and below in the ten directions, establishing himself as a Great Guide without weariness or fatigue.

Those who wish to hear the Dharma must first partake of this food. Within the three thousand great thousandfold world systems—both internal and external across the ten directions—the number of sentient beings therein is such that, despite the brilliance of the sun and moon, they cannot illuminate them; and though people possess eyes, they cannot see distant matters. Yet, for one whose ears dwell in a state of seclusion, without beholding the countenances of radiant forms, this constitutes the foremost [faculty]: all subtle matters throughout the ten directions, above, below, and within and without, shall first come to the ears!
The ear has nothing to which it is attached or delights; this is called the name "Stainless.
It contemplates all phenomena with equanimity, taking the Dharma as its sustenance; that which the ear hears first—namely, hearing the Dharma—is its primary nourishment.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva attains freedom from hunger and thirst; he takes non-hearing as food and non-seeing as drink. He regards few words as the hundred flavors, desiring purity through equanimity. His desire is like empty space—empty and free of dust—and like nirvana, it is tranquil and serene. Regarding all views as illusory transformations, this is how the Bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas with equanimity while dwelling amidst lust.
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equanimous engagement with anger?
In reality, there are no causal conditions for anger."

"Samantabhadra! Anger arises from opposition; without opposition, it does not arise. Because of dependence, opposition is produced; one falsely designates 'self' where there is no self, establishing immeasurable matters.
Just as trees grow, first from their sprouts, so too do they harbor intense and poisonous resentment; yet their sounds are naturally empty, being without perception or thought."
It is like trees in a secluded place that rub against one another while sitting; fire is ignited and burns those very trees.
Although the conditions have dispersed and each returns to its original source, the fire is extinguished and no longer appears, yet it arises from emptiness. The sound of the deer is likewise so.
Because one seeks to weigh them, both are empty; the wise understand this and do not give rise to anger. Conditions arise from sound;

they do not abide within the body, nor do they come from without. They do not arise from emptiness, nor do they arise through other conditions; they are established in opposition to one another, each being distinguished individually, categorized into various types and numbers, which lead to victory and defeat.

When Bodhisattvas observe with equanimity, they are free from anger. Just as wind passes over a field, resentment and pride may arise; yet if one knows the skillful means, one establishes conditions through mental perception.
Defiling sounds are likewise like this: anger arises from emptiness, and anger in turn burns oneself—there is no one else who can take its place.

Yet they take pride in their physical form, indulging in self-indulgence; due to their own evil speech, they sit in self-indulgent license and cannot restrain themselves. When merit is exhausted and calamity arrives, it is like the lamp of Dīpaṃkara: when the sesame oil is spent, it burns its own wick, and there is no one to save it;
such is the nature of anger.

One who can discern anger finds that it ultimately has no form or image. By observing sounds with equanimity, one realizes that the fundamental limit of anger and resentment is equal—without origin and without support. When one discerns the dharma-realm, one beholds equality. The mind arises from the four fears; grasping at the ultimate first instance of anger, one sees that anger is produced perversely through mental activity.
The mind is empty and non-existent; as soon as it arises, it ceases, having no finality.
In a state of trance, the mind cannot be consulted; to consult it would only disturb one's virtue. When the mind is rectified and free from thought, there is no lustful desire.
All desires for lust arise from the mind.
For one who is free from lust, from where could anger arise?

When the will stirs and the mind arises, the poisonous dragon is thereby created, leading to anger. As the mouth opens, transgressions enter like rivers pouring into the sea, or like a conflagration burning heaven and earth, leaving no form unexhausted. By examining the internal through successive observation, one finds nothing at all that can provoke anger.
Why is this so? Because throughout the ten directions, all are equal and there are no three miserable realms (trāya).

To have an equal mind means to be free from anger; to be free from anger means to be free from the three poisons; and if one is free from the three poisons, by what cause could they equally have illness?

As for those who are ill, they should undergo repentance. Beings in the three realms produce their forms from the mind; because of anger, they enter into this illness. If one does not reproach oneself, then for seventy-five days and seventy-five nights, one must daily and thrice self-reproach: "Now that I exist in this present life, my form is established through the actions of the mind. I have offended the people of the three realms, as well as non-human beings—whether birds or beasts—by hunting with bows and nets, or by trapping birds in cages, or by wounding and gouging their bodies, or by severing their four limbs, resulting in their current lameness and the inability of their hands and feet to function. Yet I have added further pain to them while facing them with joy."

The foolish person, not knowing themselves, brings harm upon their own body; within ten years, the body is afflicted by a grave illness, and as a result of that harm, there is no place where it can find relief.

If one gives rise to the poisonous intent of anger, even for a single moment of violent resentment, or with sword or weapon, or holding bow and arrow, desiring to strike or shoot one another, or with sickle or axe desiring to sever the head of another—raising the mind in such a manner constitutes an offense against all sentient beings of the three realms.

If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who suffers from physical illness—whether it be a minor ailment or a major one—they should regard them all as equal without distinction. They should know that they have offended the sentient beings of the triple world; therefore, according to the location of their pain, they should call out the names of the sentient beings of the triple world, deeply reproaching themselves. With disheveled hair and falling tears, they should cast themselves down and repent before the Triple Gem.

Within the Three Honored Ones there are six matters, called the Six Perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), which treat internal ailments; externally there are the Three Honored Ones, who likewise have six matters, called the Six Perfections, which treat external ailments.
Puṣya further asked:
"What are the six internal matters concerning the Three Honored Ones?
He replied:

"Regarding the three inner Honored Ones, the first is the Honored One of Mind. Within the three internal realms, he comforts sentient beings and reveals the Great Illumination, causing them all to dwell in peace and security; this is called the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Faith, and is also titled the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One."

Second is the Honored One of the Ear, who constantly dwells in a place of profound stillness, free from fetters or adornments. He soars and circulates, traveling back and forth throughout the ten directions.

Reaching every dark and remote corner of the heavens above and the earth below, there is nothing he does not hear and nothing he does not know; yet he remains without speech, tranquil and non-active. He merely moves and circulates, returning all emotions to the mind, and in each instance proclaims:
first, his words are never divergent, and thus he is named Vimalakīrti (The Stainless Renown).
Second, named Universal Upholder of the Vinaya;
third, named Broadly Opening for Deliverance;
fourth, named Great Forbearance.
Fifth, it is named the Faith of All Buddhas;
sixth, it is named the Mind of the Tathāgata;
seventh, it is named Pure and Further Pure.
Eighth, it is named Immovable;
ninth, it is named Delighting in Nothing;
tenth, it is named Vaiṇayika, the Great City that Admits Nothing.
These ten virtuous practices make one’s body identical to that of the Tathāgata.

Third is the Honored One of the Eye, who, though constantly dwelling in the realm of form and desire, does not become conceited; he leads all those who do not fly through the air, clearly perceiving the ten directions, both internally and externally, such that there is no one who can see him.
He, too, possesses ten virtuous practices: the first is named Mañjuśrī.
2. Named "Entering Everywhere";
3. Named "Purifying All Impurities";
4. Named "Ever-Pure."
Fifth, named Essence of Sun and Moon;
sixth, named Opening and Guiding All That Is Non-True;
seventh, named One Who Cannot Be Defiled.
Eighth, he is named the General Who Leads the People of the Ten Directions;
ninth, he is named One Whose Outflows Are Exhausted and Who Is Free from All Defilements;
tenth, he is named the Tathāgata Who Faithfully Protects All.
These are the three internal Honored Ones, who constantly practice great kindness and great compassion, grieving over and mindful of the suffering of birth and death.
One should know that the various classes of sentient beings within the triple world must not be disparaged.
Those who disparage have already disparaged the Three Honored Ones; yet there are still Three Honored Ones.
One should always take refuge in them, repent, and feel shame and remorse.
What are these Three Honored Ones?
First, the purity of mind is named Pāpīyan;
second, the purity of desire is named Siṃharāja;
third, the purity of form is named Garuḍa.
He asked again:
"Regarding these Three Honored Ones, what should be understood by the term 'Dharma'?
He replied:
"One who has severed the mind is free from anger and subdues all demons.
The mind is the spirit of the body; it is named Pāpīyān (in the Jin language, 'the one with manifold thoughts'), which follows and protects the heart for the sake of goodness."

The Lion King is the deity of the ear; his ears do not receive any worldly dust. Within the triple world, he alone endures all perceptions without engaging in contention with them; therefore, he is named the Lion King, which in the Jin language means "Fearless in All Things. He constantly acts as a guide for the ten directions, and for those who are to become Buddhas, he prepares seats for them without weariness or fatigue.

The Golden-Winged Bird (Garuda) is the faculty of the eye; when the eye enters into various forms, those forms are severed. Its flight through the ten directions is such that none can know it; it subdues all Māras and tramples upon all dragons.

When dragon deities wish to retaliate with thoughts of anger, the Golden-Winged Bird manifests its shadow upon the sea within the water. All the dragons are terrified and dare not come forth. When Pāpīyān raises up dragons intending to receive [the bird], the eye-faculty is already severed. The Golden-Winged Bird is above, constantly manifesting hundreds of thousands of colors like golden light, which cannot equal the essence of the bright moon; the essence of the bright moon cannot withstand the feathers of the Golden-Winged Bird. This is why the Golden-Winged Bird is uniquely supreme and heroic within the triple world.

Should there be those who act as guides and are destined to become Buddhas, I shall always be above them, illuminating them with the golden hairs of my body so that their bodies all become the color of gold; when they see one another, there shall be none who do not rejoice.
The Buddha said:
"These three honors and six persons constitute the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) of internal affairs.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the six perfections, they do not view form as being subject to impermanence."
If there were sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, then there would be no six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
If the body of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not at ease, one should know that they are in conflict with the internal six perfections and do not accord with their teaching.
You should reflect upon what was said above: this dregs-like body is merely a self-wrapped form; do not, relying on your own stubborn nature, claim that you are without fault.
If you do not repent with a sincere and earnest heart, your life will not last long, for this matter is beyond the power of even a skilled physician to cure.
Puśya again asked the Buddha:
"What are the six matters concerning the three external objects of veneration?
He replied:
"First, the Buddha is venerable;
second, the Dharma is venerable;
third, the Sangha of bhikṣus is venerable."
Furthermore, there are three Honored Ones.
What are these three?
First, the Honored One of Purity.
"Second, the Honored One of Form;
third, the Honored One of Desire.
Pu-shou asked again:
“What do these three honors correspond to?
The Buddha said:
“To abandon desire and practice giving so that one’s body attains its blessing—this is the Perfection of Giving (Dānapāramitā).”
The second is to abandon form and uphold the precepts so that the body attains purity; this is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).

The third is to abandon all worldly afflictions, practice great patience while remaining free from manifold conceptualizations, and attain pure wisdom; this is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).

The fourth is: knowing that the community of bhikṣus is pure, one abandons all matters arising from causes and conditions for cessation and establishes diligent effort, thereby reaching the site of enlightenment and dwelling on the ground of purity; this is the perfection of vigor.

The fifth is: knowing the purity of dharmas and abandoning all erroneous thoughts; by taking mental objects as conditions, one stabilizes the single mind, attains tranquility of body, and knows the past, future, and present—this is the perfection of dhyāna (dhyānapāramitā).

The sixth is: to know that the Buddha is pure, to completely relinquish all attachments, to abide nowhere at all, and to enter deeply into the essential Dharma; to be empty and free from conceptualization, realizing that the matter of nirvana is fundamentally non-existent in all respects—this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha said:
"These are the six outer perfections (pāramitās)!
One who understands these twelve matters of the inner and outer dharmas has thereby opened the twelve gates."

Although one has understanding, because it is not restrained, conceptualizations arise in response; wandering in self-indulgence, one is unable to practice forbearance. With mind, speech, and body left unrestrained, anger and harsh words constitute the twelve links of dependent origination; following the three currents of worldly convention, one does not escape the five destinies.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, neither censuring nor disparaging internal or external things, are entirely unimpeded like the form of the moon in water. They impartially examine sounds without voices of anger; they regard the limit of beginning as equal, being without beginning or limit. By discerning the dharma-realm, they behold equality.
"These bodhisattvas practice equanimity toward anger as their mental object!
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing equanimity toward ignorance?"
Folly arises from non-existence; upon examination, delusion is found to be non-existent.

If there is nothing at all, folly and delusion are fundamentally absent; thus, there is forever no madness or darkness. When a person has no corrupt aspirations, they are unimpeded like space, becoming empty, tranquil, and detached.

To conceive of obstacles while seeking emptiness is to create delusion in every direction; to establish the void as real and thereby give rise to resentment is the conduct of the ignorant. To seek fame by mastering characters and to practice for the sake of a pure reputation—such joy is difficult to attain.

All dharmas are characterized by ignorance; they take conceptualization as their object and conceptualization as their obstruction. To feel shame for that which is empty and formless is like a man wishing to cross the void without wings: his actions do not accord with the Way, he does not enter the void, and even after billions of kalpas, he shall not attain it!
One who can comprehend the uncomprehendable knows the beginning and end of emptiness; ignorance is likewise thus. The primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is inconceivable;

obscured by darkness, it does not arise. Though there is no object of intent, the dust of phenomena becomes full. It is like dwelling in empty space, where one knows neither direction nor location, and where there is neither a person of perfection nor anyone capable of delivering others across.
Those who have practiced for hundreds of thousands of billions of *kalpas* yet remain obscured by the darkness of ignorance are likewise never satisfied;

they are perpetually hungry and never satiated. Like a child, they delight in form as if it were a bladder filled with air—puffed up but empty. Liberation is nothingness within the mouth [of such delusion]. Sin and merit are like an empty bladder; seeking the supreme and the truly sublime is likewise so, and seeking the lowly and the impure is likewise so. For those who habituate themselves to folly, that which is sought can never be found.

Coming from emptiness and going to emptiness, harboring sinful desires, they take pleasure in them and do not abandon their evil ways; seeing what is good, they do not practice it, but instead focus exclusively on entering into inverted views. A practitioner who acts in this manner is called a fool without bottom.
Severing the roots and being rootless in form, there is no root and no abiding; therefore, it cannot be exhausted.
Even if the foolish could not be exhausted, delusion likewise would be unattainable. Just as sentient beings are like illusions and transformations, they cannot be bestowed.
Suppose there were a parable: the Buddha delivers all classes of sentient beings within the three realms day by day, causing them to attain nirvana.
The Buddha’s lifespan remains in the world for incalculable billions of kalpas; those he rescues, liberates, and ferries across cannot be exhausted.
Because they encounter the establishment of seeds, the human realm is without conceptualization; delusion and darkness are like illusions and thus unobtainable.
The purity of a Buddha is equal to folly and ignorance; observing them, one sees they are non-dual.

If one can practice equal contemplation, then one can recollect the Way; ignorance and wisdom are equal and one, free from all obscurations and hindrances. The various classes of sentient beings are equal and inconceivable; ignorance cannot be calculated, for when one contemplates the traces of the mind, that mind is non-existent, having no boundaries or limits. Since delusion and darkness are infinite, they cannot be apprehended.
Emptiness is nameless, yet it relies upon the existence of form; there is no one who perceives it, and it can never be grasped.
Since the nature of the mind is ignorance and is fundamentally nothing at all, from where could it arise such that anger would exist?
When one calculates that there is no self, delusion no longer arises;

what then is the nature of darkness? Just as delusion has no locus, so too is the Buddha-way: it is utterly without limit or bottom. All phenomena are non-dual; sounds are equal in their distinction. One observes the resonance of delusion with equanimity and realizes that clouds are of one kind. Ignorance is like a cloud; when one discerns this equality, one then understands the concentrated mind.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to practice equanimity regarding ignorance.
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing equanimity regarding the unwholesome?"

Desiring to practice formlessness, practicing angerlessness, and not practicing delusion; knowing that all phenomena are equal, that all sensory objects are equal, and that all arising and ceasing are entirely equal; understanding with equanimity that they are void and non-existent, empty and possessing nothing—one thus realizes purity.
"These bodhisattvas practice impartiality even toward unwholesome states.
He then addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing impartiality toward all roots of wholesome virtue?"

When sentient beings cultivate goodness, their mental activities may vary, yet all such practices are of one and the same nature; there is no practice that is not equal. By practicing with this single practice, manifesting it without obstruction, and realizing that practices are non-dual, one is then able to attain equanimity.
By knowing equality, one understands that all practices are like illusions; since form and sound are of one essence, one then comprehends vocal sounds.
Vocal sounds are non-dual, like echoes and shadows; though they come and go and circulate about, they have no fixed location, and the roots of virtue are likewise like illusory transformations.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to practice the equal engagement with the roots of all virtuous qualities.
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equal engagement with the conditioned?"
All that exists is non-existent; everything arises from thought.
Thought is empty thought; it is reckoned as immeasurable, unfathomable, boundless, and limitless—the arising of which constitutes perception.
Perception arises from the conditions of mindfulness; these enumerations are likewise inexhaustible.

One who understands equality comprehends that which is infinite: there is neither activity nor form. To explain this as equal quiescence is to behold the peace of all things; being already peaceful and already flourishing, one does not calculate them as impermanent.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to practice equanimity within the conditioned.
He then addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing equanimity within the unconditioned?"

The dharmas are fundamentally pure and quiescent, and there is no conjoining of them; the form of ignorance is merely examined through provisional sounds. Sound has neither speech nor instruction; all are understood as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). One should equally contemplate all attachments to words and sounds in this manner.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to roam equally within the unconditioned.
He then addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva roaming equally in equanimity?"

Dwelling amidst the conditioned, one does not abide in the conditioned; all formations are equal, like space, unimpeded. Not abiding in the triple world, for the triple world is fundamentally non-existent—what then is sought in nirvana?
Nirvāṇa is quiescent, neither emerging nor entering; it is beyond speech and beyond description, even unto great peace. It delivers sentient beings and resolves all distinctions.

The Dharma-body is like space: neither conjoined nor dispersed, without coming or going, and without returning; it is as empty and tranquil as space—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva’s equal wandering in equanimity.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses, which were unprecedented, in accordance with right practice, inconceivable, and rare in the world.

At that time, there were twelve thousand bodhisattvas who all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; seventy-two billion hundred-thousand devas and humans all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; two million six hundred thousand bhikṣus, having exhausted their outflows, attained liberation of mind; six thousand bhikṣuṇīs all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; and two thousand two hundred upāsakas and one thousand eight hundred upāsikās likewise all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī again addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray, O Great Sage!..."

This is the name of this samādhi; by means of it, bodhisattvas attain supreme virtue and their faculties become clear and lucid. Upon hearing the name of this samādhi and its causes, they shall obtain illumination regarding all dharmas, attaining unimpeded penetration. They will completely subdue all multitudes of deluded and heterodox views, delighting in the single syllable and discerning and understanding all syllables. By means of all syllables, they understand the single syllable; the wisdom of their eloquence is immeasurable. For the sake of all sentient beings, they preach the Dharma with discernment and clarity, attaining the patience that accords with conditions (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). Through all practices, they enter into the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), reaching the attainment of infinite and boundless discourse. They thoroughly understand the discourse on consciousness and possess the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Samantabhadra Kumārabhūta:
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!"
"I shall now analyze the origins and the end for you,
O Benevolent One. Pu-shou replied, "Excellent!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said:
"There is a samādhi named 'Detachment from Immeasurable Defilements. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they will universally perceive all forms as pure."
The Buddha told Puśya:
"There is a samādhi called 'Destroying Multiplicity. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, the radiance of their wisdom will eclipse the light of all suns and moons."

There is a samādhi named "Perfectly Accomplished Radiance. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, its majestic brilliance eclipses that of Śakra and Brahmā; all the treasures of the three realms receive peace and security, while the luminous splendors of the various devas suddenly cease to appear.
There is a samādhi called "Abandoning the Elements. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, when situated within an assembly, they eliminate all maladies of lust, anger, and delusion.
There is a samādhi named "Incapable of Being Surpassed"; if a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they will illuminate all buddha-lands throughout the eight directions, above, and below.

There is a samādhi named "The Non-arising of All Dharmas. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they will master all the scriptures of the Buddhas to instruct all beings, discerning the essential meanings for the assembled multitude and expounding upon the subtle and wondrous practice of non-attachment.

There is a samādhi named "Thunderous Sound of Non-conceptualization. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, their speech and voice will extend as far as the Brahma-heaven; among all that is proclaimed throughout the ten directions, there is none that surpasses it, and even in the profound darkness or where there are obstructions, there is nothing they do not hear.

There is a samādhi named "Illuminating All That Is Desired by the Minds of Sentient Beings. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they will bring joy to sentient beings; according to their inclinations, they cause them to be liberated from the conditions of bondage and obstruction, so that the entire assembly universally attains peace and security.

There is a samādhi named "Manifesting Joy through Unconverging Diligence. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they behold the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and perceive that there are no finite limits to the delusions of beginning and end; whatever they hear or see, they penetrate thoroughly, and there is nothing among all that enters their experience that can surpass it.

There is a samādhi named "Treasure-Virtue Delighting in the World of Non-Thought. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they exercise various supernormal powers to transform and benefit sentient beings.

There is a samādhi named "Convergence of All Sounds. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they awaken to all speech and sounds; by means of non-dual syllables, they comprehend a single syllable, and with a single syllable, they expound upon non-dual syllables. By comprehending internal syllables and external syllables, they realize that while the internal is not reached, the external is likewise not comprehended; yet when the internal and external correspond, there are no differing characters.

There is a samādhi called "Accumulation of All Meritorious Virtues. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they discern between transgressions and blessings, manifesting impartiality, and greatly gladdening all sentient beings. They cause them to hear the voice of the Buddha, the voice of the Dharma, the voices of the śrāvakas, the voices of the pratyekabuddhas, the voices of the bodhisattvas, the voice of the perfections (pāramitās), and the voice of omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Yet, in what they teach, there is no sound; they fully comprehend the profound and essential activity of all things.

There is a samādhi called "The Arising of All Dhāraṇīs as the King of All. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they will discern all immeasurable dhāraṇīs and the essentials of manifold wisdom, causing all unimpeded dharmas to become clearly manifest.

There is a samādhi called "Purifying All Eloquence through Unconditioned Practice. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, all sounds and speech are stilled and eliminated; there is no verbal instruction, nor is there any resonance. There is neither word nor teaching, and nothing at all exists.
Thereupon, Viśeṣamati addressed the World-Honored One:
"Indeed, O Great Sage!
Would this humble body be fit to expound the merit of these scriptural teachings?"
He said, "You should preach.
Puśya addressed the Buddha:

"If a bodhisattva hears this sutra and does not harbor doubt, but resolves to receive, uphold, recite, chant, and read it, that person shall, in the present life, attain wondrous eloquence—eloquence of intelligence, eloquence of joy, and profound and subtle eloquence—without impediment. They shall constantly practice a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, never again harboring thoughts of malice."
"Why is this? Even if one were to contemplate the course of actions performed and practice those deeds, knowing the truths as they follow the person, one would never abandon them.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Puśya:
“Excellent, excellent!
You have spoken these words most skillfully; they are indeed as you intend.

For example, just as practicing generosity leads to great wealth without falsehood, and observing the precepts leads to rebirth in heaven without falsehood, so too shall it be with this sutra: studying it will lead to eloquence without falsehood, and one will fully realize their original aspiration, just as when the sun rises and shines upon the world, all darkness is entirely dispelled.”

This sutra is likewise; those who recite and study it will come to possess eloquence such that nothing remains unmastered, just as a bodhisattva seated at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree attains the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, achieving supreme perfect awakening.
In this way, a bodhisattva who studies and recites this sutra will certainly attain eloquence and eliminate all doubts. Therefore, Puṣya!

If a bodhisattva wishes to manifest eloquence and become thoroughly proficient in all dharmas, upon hearing this sutra, their mind shall not waver; they should immediately receive, uphold, explain, and chant it, extensively expounding its meaning for the sake of the assembled multitude.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"After the parinirvāṇa, should there be those who receive, uphold, recite, or expound this Dharma-sūtra, and who spread its meaning for the sake of the assembly, I shall personally proclaim and explain for them their destination, so that they may be free from doubt and swiftly attain eloquence."
At that time, the evil Māra, overcome with grief and distress, shed tears as he approached the Buddha and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"May this sutra not be established! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, always harbors great compassion; to those who suffer and are afflicted, he bestows great peace."
How fortunate I am, O Great Sage!
I pray that you will dispel my delusions,
just as the World-Honored One of old sat beneath the tree at the site of enlightenment and expounded this scriptural Dharma.
Now, as you once again preach this sutra,
I am filled with sorrow and my heart is burdened with distress.
When the Tathāgata first attained the Way of the Buddha and was engaged in saving and delivering beings, I could not restrain my inner turmoil and agitation.

All shall attain the stage of non-retrogression, reach the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment. Any sentient beings who hear this sutra with their ears, listen to its sound, or receive its name, shall all attain the Way and reach nirvana.
"The realm of emptiness and selflessness shall empty the palaces of the Māras.
The Great Sage nurtures all beings and establishes great compassion; he looks only upon us with pity and seeks to save us.
The Buddha addressed the Māra, saying:
“Pāpīyān! Do not fear, do not be terrified, do not be anxious!
It is not because all sentient beings have been completely extinguished that the Tathāgata has established this sutra.”
Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, Māra leaped for joy; a wholesome mind arose within him, and he suddenly vanished.
Viśiṣṭacāritra addressed the Buddha:
“For what reason did you deliver this teaching to Māra?”
The Buddha told Puśya:
"This sūtra abides in non-abiding; therefore, Māra speaks these words:
'I do not establish this sūtra!'"
This is most sincere and not false.
All dharmas abide in non-abiding; they cannot be attained, they are beyond verbal instruction, they are free from duality, and their original limit is equal.

When one realizes that all things are fundamentally without origin, the Dharma-realm is like a scale, as level as empty space; it is without preference or aversion, truly and perfectly without distinction.
Now that this sutra circulates throughout Jambudvīpa, there shall surely be auspicious omens throughout the world.

Just as the World-Honored One had established this teaching of ultimate truth, a voice spontaneously resounded throughout the air, heard everywhere: "It is truly as the Buddha has said; it is sincere and not false.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Receive these essentials of the 'Universal Gate' Chapter of the Sūtra; uphold, recite, read, and proclaim them to your fellow students."
He further said:
"Ānanda! This treasury of eighty-four thousand dharma-categories, when compared to this scripture, is equal to it without any distinction."

Why is this so? Because a single phrase of this sutra universally enters the gates of immeasurable wisdom; the essential points of the entire dharma realm can only be discerned and fully understood by the Tathāgata.
When sentient beings understand this sutra and thereby attain the path of Buddhahood, they shall thereafter expound the eighty-four thousand collections of various sūtras and treasuries.
For this reason, Ānanda!
"You should receive this sutra with care, and you must hold it fast, recite it, and chant it.

Having spoken these words to the assembly, the Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha, the youth Mañjuśrī, the venerable Ānanda, as well as the devas, humans, gandharvas, and asuras, rejoiced upon hearing the sutra; they bowed their heads in prostration and withdrew.
The Universal Gate Chapter Spoken by the Buddha
